# Copper December 2012 - Having rallied some three percent over the course of two trading days at the end of November, the copper price failed to build on this momentum and cash quotes generally ebbed back and forth around the $8000/t level in the final month of 2012. Inevitably, December tends to be characterised by a winding down of activity and a general reluctance to take significant trading positions and this proved to be the case again this year. - The most encouraging development this month is that there are finally clear signs of an upturn in Chinese copper demand. Capacity utilisation rates in the wire and cable, wire rod and tube segments all accelerated noticeably in November and local market reports indicate this momentum has continued into December. Even so, we have been compelled to downgrade our estimate of Chinese refined consumption in 2012 to 5.0% from 6.25% previously, as the upturn has come slightly later and with less vigour than we had anticipated. However, Wood Mackenzie has maintained the forecast of 8.5% growth in 2013, even though the net tonnage addition is slightly reduced due to the lower base effect. The net impact of other changes is to reduce our world refined consumption growth estimate from 1.2% to 1.0% for 2012, followed by an unchanged 5.1% expansion in 2013, driven principally by the rebound in China. - Unusually for this time of year there is little progress to report in the long-term market. Last November, Freeport had already concluded a number of deals including its first with Jiangxi Copper at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb. At present, rumours suggest that the miner has been far less active in the market leading some observers to opine that there is little advantage in Freeport being the first to settle, only to be undercut in subsequent deals. That said recent press reports suggest that Japan’s Pan Pacific Copper is set to agree terms with an unnamed mining company. The terms of the deal are unconfirmed, but are said to be in the range $70-79/t & 7.0-7.9c/lb. per Monthly Update ## Market Developments Having rallied some three percent over the course of two trading days at the end of November, the copper price failed to build on this momentum and cash quotes generally ebbed back and forth around the $8000/t level in the final month of 2012. Inevitably, December tends to be characterised by a winding down of activity and a general reluctance to take significant trading positions and this proved to be the case again this year. **Emerging consensus on China outlook** The rise in cash quotes in the final days of November were primarily on hopes for a soft landing from the US fiscal cliff, although US dollar softness and technical trading factors also buoyed market sentiment. Against this positive backdrop, prices ought to have moved meaningfully higher, especially after Chinese PMI data moved above the 50 expansionary threshold but in the event prices only edged upwards. A consensus appears to be emerging in commodity markets that China’s economy has turned the corner. In copper this is not just manifesting itself in improving underlying demand and declining inventories of finished goods but also in consumption of cathode. **Mixed signals on US fiscal cliff** There has been less of a consensus on whether the US will avoid its fiscal cliff. Initially the view was that hopes for a swift and decisive resolution to US lawmakers’ disagreements was boosting or at least underpinning sentiment, while more recently concern of a fall over the edge was said to be tempering gains or accentuating losses. Amid the market flip flopping on the US situation, Europe tried to rest the attention away after the European Central Bank painted a bleak outlook for the Eurozone economies. Shortly after, Prime Minister Mario Monti announced his resignation and Sivlio Berlusconi said that he wanted the Italian Job, blowing the doors off hopes that the region’s debt crisis had been contained. **Self preservation caps price movements** Even in the face of the mixed backdrop amid conflicting fundamental factors, it would seem that hopes for a Chinese recovery prevailed. This led to new longs entering the market through the first two weeks of the month, according to our analysis of open interest data and price movements. This was also confirmed by the release of the commitments of traders report from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which showed that shorts had reduced their positions and longs increased to result in net longs being in the ascendency overall. Ultimately though, self preservation put a limit on sustained price movements in either direction as traders wished to avoid getting caught out in thinning trade ahead of the Christmas and New Year holidays. As a result, prices were little change for the month overall. #### **CFTC copper positions** '000 Contracts

**Exchange stocks move higher at year end** With prices being underpinned on the downside by increasing confidence on the Chinese outlook, the market shrugged off the increase in exchange stocks over the course of the month. It is likely that the rise in these inventories did not significantly temper sentiment because deliveries have occurred predominantly in locations where it will be difficult to source cathodes easily or indeed quickly. As such, the uplift in total LME stocks is not a reflection of increased availability of those stocks. Total LME inventories stood at 251kt at the end of November but had jumped to 312kt as of 19th of December following increases in Europe, North America and Asia. In Europe, there were deliveries into Antwerp where moves appear to be afoot to build a queue for withdrawal, while the rise in registered tonnage in Rotterdam would appear to be producers, consumers and traders offloading material at their financial year end. In the US, deliveries into New Orleans accounted for the increase in North American LME inventory, with this seemingly down to warehousing companies wishing to get copper behind queues of other material, while COMEX stocks increased only marginally from 58kt in November to 63kt now. Similarly, there was a moderate increase Metals Market Service Monthly Update - December 2012 Page 2 of 22 Copper Monthly Update in SHFE material, which edged up to 205kt. It is our opinion that this 205kt accounts for most of the difference between the widely reported 1 million tonnes of bonded warehouse stocks and our estimate of closer to 750-800kt. We assume a miscommunication led to a total SHFE and bonded figure being erroneously reported as the bonded stocks level, which has since circulated in the market. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

**Physical ETF wins SEC approval** In the middle of the month JPMorgan received SEC approval for its physically backed copper ETF following a two year wait and opposition from consumers. The fear among dissenters is that the $5Bn (and c.62kt of copper) fund would mop up stocks in an already tight market and as a consequence drive prices and premia higher and increase volatility for consumers already struggling to finance their own inventory. Significantly, the higher storage costs and other fees of owning a physically backed copper ETF relative to gaining exposure through Futures, means that such a product needs to rise more in value in order to cover these costs. In any case, our expectations of copper prices weakening over the next few

years as a result of increases in mine supply that are coming on stream somewhat diminish the attractiveness of gaining “long” exposure to copper. The best chance for a physically backed product was around two years ago when one was launched, however, this fund only holds around 2kt of copper currently. Assuming we are correct in our assertions, it is unlikely that the JPMorgan product will have a significant impact on the copper market. **Premia little changed as buying interest wanes** Waning cathode consumption as semis producers and their customers wind down output ahead of the year end has tempered already sluggish demand in many key markets and as a result, premia have edged lower. Nowhere is this more typified than in Europe, where 2012 was a year to forget for most metal consumers. Rotterdam cathode premia remained around the $80/t level on a combination of sluggish spot purchasing and significant deliveries of material into exchange warehouses. In the US, premia are broadly at the same levels as last month of around 5.5-6.0c/lb in very quiet spot demand, although consumers do at least feel more confident than in Europe about booking contracts for next year. These have tended to be at similar-to-slightly larger volumes to 2012, with consumers increasingly concerned that warehouses in the US are no longer a viable source, given the lengthening queues and hence timeframes to withdraw material. There has been a noticeable improvement in Chinese cathode demand and underlying conditions in general in that country, although this has done little to improve premia amid high burgeoning stock levels. In fact, copper premia edged slightly lower in December to $35-65/t as healthier demand conditions have been bettered by record refined copper production and a rebound in imports in November. Bonded stocks could well be drawn down in the first half of next year on improving demand and this will likely result in apparent consumption figures looking artificially low also. In tandem with strengthening consumption through the first quarter and in particular after the Chinese New Year, and sequential gains in the usually seasonally strong Q2, bonded stocks should fall. For 2012 as a whole we estimate net imports of refined copper of 3.2Mt, after accelerated growth in the first half, although we forecast a decline to 2.4Mt next year. This raises the question of how our 8.5% and c.700kt increase in Chinese demand will be met? We forecast a rise in imports of concentrate, blister and scrap into China which will help boost refined production, while we also foresee the potential for a drawdown of cathode stocks in China to the tune of 250kt that would contribute to meeting this requirement. The anticipated sequential improvement in demand through the first half of next year in China and on a global basis should result in prices peaking in the second and third quarters at $7850/t before the increase in mine supply that we forecast for 2013 as a whole brings pressure to bear in the form of upward momentum on metal inventories in tandem with a downgrading of cash quotes by Q4. For 2013 we forecast prices will average $7725/t, down from an estimated $7948/t in 2012 as the market surplus builds from 173kt to 256kt. The 2013 surplus is lower than previously forecast in part because we have now increased our forecast disruption allowance from 5% to 6%, which has lowered production. We have made this change as we feel that this will be a more representative outcome with the prospect of a number of new projects coming on line in 2013 plus the potential for strikes. Time will tell, but it may be that this figure could prove conservative. The largest disruption to initial mine production capability was 8% in 2008 and today, a 1% change in the disruption allowance is equivalent to a ~200kt change in our metal balance. Aside from the obvious threat to supply growth there are also other risks to our forecasts for the coming year. Following significant destocking of Chinese semis and fabricated products, 2013 could see a major restocking along the demand chain which would have a leveraged and substantial impact on the country’s first use consumption. Under such a scenario it is possible for an uplift in Chinese consumption to register double-digit growth. A 1% change in Chinese consumption affects the metal market balance by 80kt. Conversely, the release of speculative metal stocks from Chinese bonded warehouses back into the market or onto exchanges could impact negatively on the physical feel to the market despite our relatively modest surplus predicted for next year as a whole. Although we think it unlikely, any easing of monetary policy, particularly bank lending, initiated by the new Chinese government within the higher end of the property market could be the catalyst for such an outcome. Looking to the very short term some minor volatility could be expected in the first half of January as commodity indices change their weightings. That said the adjustments for copper are fairly minor with the S&P GSCI index to increase the weight of copper from 3.24% to 3.28%, while the Dow Jones – UBS Commodity Index will increase the share of copper from 7.1% to 7.3%. Funds that track these indices account for around three quarters of money invested in commodities, although the rebalancing tend to take place over a number of days to avoid causing undue turbulence. Capacity utilisation rates in the wire and cable, wire rod and tube segments all accelerated noticeably in November and local market reports indicate this momentum has continued into December. Even so, we have been compelled to downgrade our estimate of Chinese refined consumption in 2012 to 5.0% from 6.25% previously, as the upturn has come slightly later and with less vigour than we had anticipated. However, Wood Mackenzie has maintained the forecast of 8.5% growth in 2013, even though the net tonnage addition is slightly reduced due to the lower base effect. The net impact of other changes is to reduce our world refined consumption growth estimate from 1.2% to 1.0% for 2012, followed by an unchanged 5.1% expansion in 2013, driven principally by the rebound in China. ### **China** **Downgrade to 2012 refined consumption growth** Last month we lowered our projection of Chinese refined consumption growth in 2012 from 6.25% to 5.0%. Although we finally saw in November the first tangible signs of an upturn in copper wire and cable demand that we had been expecting in the fourth quarter, the impact on the copper rod business has not been as great as anticipated. Due to weaker demand from end users, wire and cable production slowed in October from the higher levels that had been seen in August and September. Faced with the lack of follow through orders, a number of the smaller and mid-sized rod mills choose to idle their lines through the October national holiday week, leading to a decline in average industry u

tilisation.  The weakness of the market also led to the suspension of output at Xiangrui’s new 300kta capacity rod mill due to the lack of orders. 

**A November rebound in wire and cable…** November registered the first meaningful signs of a general upturn in Chinese market activity.  There was a distinct increase in orders for both power cable and winding wire, two of the largest volume product lines in the Chinese market, suggesting that a broad based improvement may at last be gaining some momentum.  Utilisation rates in the wire and cable industry reached their highest level so far this year at just under 80%, compared to 71% in the early part of 2012.  Although there is some evidence that the stimulus measures announced earlier this year may be starting to take effect, there is also the belief that the widespread industry destocking of final inventories may be coming to an end, enabling new orders to be placed to refill the supply chain.  Power cable demand has benefitted recently from some strong sequential gains in power grid investment.  Expenditure surged by 32% monthon-month in September, followed by a 36% month-on-month increase in October.  This is in response to the release of orders after the fifth round of bidding for power cables contracts from the State Power Grid in late-September.  The improvement in winding wire demand is due to a combination of continuing healthy orders from the automotive sector and accelerating offtake from the home appliance sector now that the worst effects of finished inventory overhang appear to be past.  The clearest evidence for this is to be found in the AC industry where final stocks of 6.9M units fell below monthly production of 10.4M units in October.  This echoes the wider improvement in the Chinese manufacturing sector with November factory output reaching its highest level so far this year. 

**…feeds through into wire rod** The increase in wire and cable production led to a 5-10% sequential monthly increase in wire rod output according to a sample of individual mill’s production plans.  For those mills that shut for one week in October the increase was closer to 10-15%.  A recent survey of rod producers confirmed that average capacity utilisation rose from 69% in October to 74% in November and that utilisation levels would likely maintain this higher level in December.  Tianjin North China Electric Wire announced that it would likely modestly exceed its rod production target of 160kta in 2012 after output rose in the fourth quarter.  However ‘fierce competition’ has restricted the company from operating anyway near to its 240kta capacity.  More optimistic news comes from industry leader Jiangxi Copper which expects to exceed its annual rod production target by 10% this year.  The company now aims to make 407kta of rod in 2012 against its original plan of 370kta. 

**Other product segments are stable but should improve in 2013** Despite the recent double digit increases in floor space under co

nstruction and completions, Chinese building wire consumption was reported to be stable in October and November.  Cold weather is now beginning to affect construction activity in the northern provinces and this will progressively restrict sales in those regions until March.  Copper tube and pipe consumption has been on a declining trend since May and fell further in October as a result of shutdowns at air conditioner plants for the national holidays. However, there is much more optimism for the year ahead with industry leader Golden Dragon projecting a 13.4% rebound in its tube production up to 400kt in 2013 after an expected 5.4% decline to 350kt in 2012.  The company expects an improvement in domestic demand as well as increased export orders to Japan, South East Asia and Europe. Golden Dragon had been forced to cut its inventories of refined copper and finished products to ease the financing burden of its working capital requirements.  Sheet and strip consumption for high end sophisticated products in complex alloys has strengthened but demand for standard coppers and brasses for leadframes and connectors is stable. Manufacturers do not anticipate any material improvement until the usual seasonal spring upturn in 2013. 

**Consumption accelerates in 2013 followed by normalisation of growth** Buoyed by the stronger finish to 2012, with semis production exceeding 1Mt in September, October and November, Wood Mackenzie continues to forecast a faster 8.5% acceleration in refined consumption in 2013.  Year-on-year comparisons should be very favourable for the first three quarters of 2013, and especially so in Q2 against a period when the seasonal upturn failed to materialise in 2012. Moreover, now that the change in government has been completed, it is likely that we will see further stimulus measures

announced to secure the economic recovery and increase copper demand.  Aside from the anticipated pick up in underlying demand there have also been several project announcements which should be to the structural benefit of future consumption.  Jiangxi Jinhong Metal Co. released news that it will build a 200kta bright copper rod project in Gangbei district of Guigang city.  This was followed by news that Daye Nonferrous Ruixin Copper Co. will also construct a 200kta rod mill.  Ruixin Copper Co. is a subsidiary of Changzhou Daijang Copper Co..  Meanwhile the Tongling Nonferrous Metals Group has confirmed that it has selected Contirod technology for its previously announced 225kta rod project in Tongling, Anhui province.  Commissioning of the line is scheduled for autumn 2013.  And in the last week, Gansu Baiyin Nonferrous has revealed that it will be building a 150kt capacity rod mill. 

December has seen a tangible change in economic sentiment that should prove favourable for broader Chinese copper consumption prospects in 2013.  The Shanghai composite shar

e index posted a 4.3% single day gain on December 14<sup>th</sup> , the largest rise since October 2009, as investors were boosted by news that the new government will soon announce measures to boost urbanisation which should fuel the rebound in manufacturing activity.  It was said that the government will promote “sustained and healthy development”, accompanied by a “prudent” monetary policy and a “proactive” fiscal stance. 

### **United States** 

**Macroeconomic news is encouraging** US GDP grew at an annualized rate of 2.0% in Q3 2012 a little quicker than the 1.3% annualized rate achieved in Q2.  The latest data from the current quarter is also supportive of a gradually improving macroeconomic picture.  October housing starts rose 3.6% month-on-month to 894,000 units, at a yearly rate, the fastest since July 2008, while the year-on-year growth rate hit an impressive 41.9%.  Single family dwelling unit starts were broadly flat on a month-on-month basis with the majority of the increase being seen in multi-dwelling units.  Housing completions also showed a broadly similar trend, with a notable feature being the strong concentration of growth in the South, with moderate growth in the West and Mid-West but continued weakness in the North East. 

**Turning point must be nearing in construction products** Building wire sellers reported mixed trends consistent with a turning point having been reached or being close by.  Encore Wire registered a 2.7% year-on-year decline in Q3 shipments of building wire, measured on a copper content basis, however this did represent a moderate 1.6% sequential increase from Q2.  Encore Wire’s comments on the results were, “The third quarter of this year was another fairly steady volume quarter in the midst of this construction industry recession.  There are bright spots around the country and talk of some major projects, but for the most part we are still in the trough.  Major projects are discussed but then get delayed due to uncertainties surrounding the global economy, the US economy and political environment.  The good news is that our volumes are not trending downwards”.  Building wire inventories remain lean throughout the supply chain, indicating that any increase in underlying demand should quickly translate into higher wire production and rod demand.  The repairs and remodelling to damaged houses in New York and New Jersey caused by Hurricane Sandy should also be positive for volumes in 2013.  Nexans reported some sales gains in its North American (US and Canada) distributors and installers business segment in Q3.  Meanwhile General Cable said its business performed more or less as expected, although it did complete the acquisition of Alcan Cable North America to boost its product offering in cost competitive aluminium construction wire and cable.  Brass mill products destined primarily for the construction sector have also yet to show a recovery.  Brass rod output fell 0.3% year-on-year in the year to Sept

ember, while copper tube production dropped 5.4% over the same period. **Copper rod output follows erratic trend** After the impressive months of July and August, when US rod production rose respectively by 5.4% and 7.4% year-on-year, the recent trend in output has been more disappointing. Production fell by 0.7% year-on-year in September and then declined by 2.4% year-on-year in October. Wire rod demand is reported to have stagnated in the two months prior to the close fought US Presidential election as business confidence weakened due to the uncertainty of the outcome and its unclear impact on the US economy. Also, the new SDI La Farga rod mill appears to have been less of a force in the marketplace so far than might have been expected. It is clearly taking time to convince potential customers that its scrap feed based wire rod is a viable potential alternative to the traditional cathode quality rod that they are used to handling. A company official was quoted as saying that the new facility is in limited production. “We’ve produced quality rod and are in the process of getting approval of customers and we have done so with several customers”. But that they were, “Waiting for more customer orders to start producing more”. Total US rod production will likely fall below 220Mlbs (100kt/m) in both November and December reflecting the usual seasonal year-end downturn. **Brass mill products – some optimism in flat rolled products** In the year to September US production of copper plate, sheet and strip rose by 2.3% year-on-year, while output of copper alloy plate, sheet and strip climbed by 2.5%. The third quarter was a strong one for industry leader Olin Brass, a division of Global Brass & Copper Holdings Inc., which reported a 10.0% year-on-year surge in its third quarter shipment volumes. However, this was partly offset by a 6.3% decline in sales through the holding company’s AJ Oster servicenter operations. Despite challenging end use market conditions, sheet and strip demand has benefitted from healthy sales to the interconnect market. ### **Brazil** **Economic outlook downgrades growth prospects** Brazilian GDP grew at the anaemic rate of just 0.6% in the third quarter of 2012, well below consensus economic opinion. The state statistics agency also halved its first and second quarter GDP estimates to leave 2012 annual growth at a 2.4% rate compared to the government forecast of 4.7%. The outcome is all the more depressing

because the government has aggressively lowered interest rates down to 7.25%, cut taxes and boosted expenditure over the past year in an effort to stimulate the economy.  It leaves the country facing its worst two-year growth performance in a decade.  The one bright spot is retail sales which rose for the fourth consecutive month and surged 8.5% from a year-ago.  Vehicle sales reached a record 420,100 units in August due to a sales tax reduction that the government has extended to the year end in order to support the sector.  One of the main problems the country faces is the lack of investment by industry. As a result the government has started to focus on resolving the long standing bottlenecks in transport, infrastructure and utilities designed to take Brazil into a “new phase” of economic development by boosting competitiveness. 

**Domestic copper industry sales forecast lowered** Faced with the deteriorating economic situation, the country’s national association for the copper, semi-manufactures and wire and cable industries has been forced to revise down its sales expectations on two separate occasions to reflect the disappointing volume of business.  ABC Sindicel began the year with a 5% growth target, but reduced this to 3% at mid-year, and subsequently to 2.2-2.3%.  It had been expected that the building projects and the infrastructure investment for the Football World Cup and the Olympics would have begun to stimulate copper semis and wire and cable consumption this year.  However, although these projects have begun they have not yet reached the stage when copper procurement is required.  Moreover demand from the construction, oil and gas, telecommunication and automotive industries has also been below earlier expectations. 

**Paranapanema outperforms as it implements a new corporate strategy** In August 2012 the group’s management announced its “Nova Paranapanema” project with the aim of consolidating its leadership in the Brazilian copper business, expanding the scale of its business and divesting non-core assets.  In early October the Group completed the sale of its fertilisers subsidiary Cibrafertil to the Colombian company OFD Holding enabling it to concentrate on expanding its copper business.  Paranapanema is mid-way through an expansion at its copper refinery at Dias D’Avila which will see capacity rise from 220kta to 280kta by Q1 2013.  Its new industrial copper tube plant should also commission at the same time in Utinga Sao Paulo which will double the company’s capacity to 36kta.  Cold rolling capacity for flat rolled products at the same plant is also due to be upgraded from 28kta to 55kta through the technological modernisation of the production facilities.  A further ambitious project, to establish a new hot rolling mill in Sao Mateus, Espirito Santo state, is under technical review with a capacity of up to 200kta being considered.  Thus far its new policy is having a broadly favourable outcome despite the economic backdr

op.  Sales of wire rod and drawn wire rose 22.5% from 77kt to 94kt in Q1-Q3 2012 compared to the prior year period, but the company’s brass mill output dropped from 46kt to 45kt over the same timeframe.  Paranapanema is also hoping that a favourable implementation of Brazilian Senate Resolution No.13, which would reduce the tax breaks currently afforded to imported competitor copper products would also help stimulate its production and sales domestically in 2013. 

**Termomecanica has also expanded its capacity** Privately-owned Termomecanica has also been expanding its downstream capabilities, both within and outside of Brazil.  Domestically it has invested in a third plant in the city of Sao Bernardo do Campo for a scrap based Properzi wire rod line to diversify its product range beyond brass mill products.

Externally it acquired Cembrass in 2011, with its brass rod operations in Chile and Argentina.  Capacity in Argentina has been expanded from 5kta to 9kta while that in Chile has been increased from 15kta to 27kta in anticipation of market expansion.  Interestingly, Termomecanica’s management was quoted as stating publicly that is not in favour of a change in the tax breaks on imports, on the grounds that it would afford Paranapanema an unfair advantage in the refined copper market domestically as the only producer.  It would prefer that the current status is maintained for refined copper, though presumably the company would still be in favour of the removal of tax breaks on imported downstream products. Termomecanica has an annual production of around 90kt of copper and alloy products. 

### **Europe** 

**Slow end to a disappointing 2012** Activity in the European market has unsurprisingly been very subdued as we approach the year end.  Consumers have long been operating with minimal inventory levels so there is little in the way of additional destocking to be done in readiness for year-end.  Given the obscured economic outlook, there is little if any consensus on the consumption outlook for 2013.  The hope is that the regional economy will avoid the sort of shock that befell it in 2012 and this will pave the way for stabilisation which can then be a platform for a modest recovery, initially led by restocking. 

**Little change expected in short term market dynamics** At this point in time, there is little evidence to suggest there will be any departure away from the prevailing micro trends in demand from a geographic or end use market perspective. Consumption continues to hold up reasonably well in Russia and Poland, led by competitively priced wire rod exports and aided by fairly resilient domestic consumption.  Scandinavia continues to perform well economically with power cable demand supported by a number of inter-country grid interconnection schemes, submarine power cable orders and uncompleted offshore wind farm projects.  Utilities and o

perators in Northern Europe have been the most active exponents of realising the potential of renewable energy and in unlocking the prospects for energy trading which a flexible interconnected grid offers. Domestic demand in Southern Europe, particularly in Italy and Spain, continues to weaken in the construction and home appliance end use segments. There is little to suggest that there will be any reversal of this trend over the winter months. However, export sales of wire rod into the recovering North African market have supported first use consumption. **Slow progress in the long-term market** Unusually for this time of year there is little progress to report in the long-term market.  Last November, Freeport had already concluded a number of deals including its first with Jiangxi Copper at $63.5/t & 6.35c/lb.  At present, rumours suggest that the miner has been far less active in the market leading some observers to opine that there is little (and

perhaps no) advantage in Freeport being the first to settle, only to be undercut in subsequent deals, particularly in China and India as was the case in 2011. Thus far in 2012 BHPBilliton, acting on behalf of Escondida, is thought to be the only supplier to have tabled terms, apparently ranging from $60/t & 6c/lb to $63/t & 6.3c/lb with various Asian smelters. For their part, buyers are looking for numbers around the $80/t & 8c/lb mark. A key issue for the custom smelting sector is that with Freeport seemingly in a ‘wait and see’ mode, there is no obvious supplier to turn to for numbers that might provide an alternative to BHPBilliton’s. One would imagine that Antofagasta and Teck will be looking to establish a high-grade premium after a benchmark for medium grade concentrates has been negotiated (for Los Pelambres and HVC), while Codelco probably does not view itself as a dominant seller given the size of its long-term book. Meanwhile, Anglo’s more pressing objective will be to establish tonnage deferrals on its Collahuasi and Los Bronces deliveries in the wake of production issues at these two key mining assets. **Green light for Aktogay** Kazakhmys has announced that following completion of a successful feasibility study, it has approved construction of the Aktogay project in south eastern Kazakhstan.  Production of SxEw cathode from oxide ore is forecast to start in 2015, with output of copper in concentrate from underlying sulphide ore to follow a year later. Combined production is expected to average just over 100kt/a over the first 10 years of the mine’s life, with an average of 22kt/a being in the form of SxEw cathode.  The estimated capital cost of $2Bn is to be primarily funded through a $1.5Bn finance facility from the China Development Bank.  Development of Aktogay project, along with the Boschekul project which was approved last year will enable Kazakhmys to increase their production of mined copper from around 300kt in 2012 to 500kt/a by the end of the decade.

The plant is scheduled to come into operation towards the end of 2016 and is understood to be designed to produce ~60kt/a of copper in concentrate. **Resolution setback** Planned **s** haft development and drilling activity at the Resolution project in Arizona is to be scaled back in 2013 due to delays in securing a land swap necessary for the mine’s development.  The project, which is a joint venture between Rio Tinto (51%) and BHPBilliton (49%), is dependant upon the US Congress passing a ‘Land Exchange’ bill whereby land held by Resolution Copper would be traded for publicly held land known as Oak Flats, which is required to develop the project.  The Oak Flats area is considered sacred by the local Apache population and is protected from development under legislation passed by President Dwight Eisenhower in 1955.  Rio Tinto is reported to have cut its 2013 development budget allocated to the project by 75% to $50M.  The project, which would entail development of a block cave mine, is forecast to produce 500kt/a of copper in concentrate.  It is estimated that at least 10 year’s of development work would be required between the passing of the ‘Land Swap’ legislation and the start of production.
